headline: Bone age
subhead: IS IT MEASURING THE RIGHT BONES?

headline: The basics
body: So bone age is read from an X-ray of your hand and wrist. One image, one number, and that number then gets used to estimate how much growth you have left in your entire skeleton. | Sounds reasonable until you look at what the hand is actually doing compared to your legs.
punch: Your hand is not where your height comes from.

headline: The mechanism
body: A very important study, Dolan et al in PLOS Biology, looked at *epiphyseal fusion*, which is the growth plate closing for good, in different bones of the same animal. In mice the phalanges fused at **3 weeks** and the metacarpals at **4 weeks**. | The tibia and femur had still not fused at **12 weeks**. Same animal, same genetics, completely different timing.
punch: _The small bones close first. Every time._

headline: Same in rats
subhead: THIS IS NOT A MOUSE THING
body: They repeated it in rats and got the exact same order. **12 weeks** in the phalanges, **16 weeks** in the metacarpals, and the tibias and femurs still open at 16. | What this means is that the hand finishing early is a feature of how the skeleton works, not a quirk of one species.

headline: The nuances
subhead: THEY ALSO GROW AT DIFFERENT SPEEDS
body: Now here is the part most people miss. At one week old, the metacarpal bone growth rate was **49%** of the tibial rate, and the *proliferation rate per column*, meaning how many times the cells in one column of the growth plate divide, was **46%**. | So the hand bones are not just finishing earlier. They are slower the entire time.
punch: ==Your hand bones grow at half the speed of your legs.==

headline: Why?
body: Every marker of *growth plate senescence*, which is the plate slowly running out of divisions, was more advanced in the metacarpals and phalanges than in the femurs and tibias. | The most shocking part was the reason. They took *chondrocytes* out of finger bones and leg bones, and the finger cells divided slower. Then they added IGF-1 to the finger cells and proliferation rose **to match the untreated leg cells**.
punch: The bone is the same. The signal reaching it is not.

headline: In humans
body: Now lets look at the human data. Kvist 2021 did MRI on **958 people** aged 14 to 21 and imaged the wrist, knee and ankle in every person. The results showed that fusion timing varied by site inside the same body, and that complete fusion happened about **2 years earlier** in girls. | So even in humans, one body has several closure dates.

headline: What predicts it
body: *Pubertal stage* correlated with fusion at every site they imaged. Wrist **0.596**, upper shin **0.597**, ankle **0.598**, heel **0.514** in males, lower but present in females. | This means where you are in puberty is the variable to track, and the hand X-ray is reading the bones that are furthest through it.
punch: Track your puberty stage, not your birthday.

headline: The part nobody covers
body: The same study tested two more things. **BMI correlated** with growth plate maturity, 0.186 to 0.384. **Physical activity** had no significant correlation in males at any site, and in females one very low correlation at the wrist, **0.095**, nothing else. | Everyone talks about training. In the largest human imaging study on this, training barely registered.
punch: ==Being heavier tracked faster maturation. Training did not.==

headline: How do we use this
body: So from these studies we know three things. The hand finishes first. Puberty stage tracks fusion better than anything else measured. And body composition, not training, is what tracked faster maturation. | To use this, read your bone age as an estimate from your fastest ageing bones, not a readout of your legs, and track your pubertal stage.
